key_terms.meaning: The physical process being controlled — a motor, a furnace, a water tank (chapter 1).
The element that decides the actuator command from the reference and the measured output (chapter 1).
The device that converts the controller's command into the physical input the plant needs, such as a valve or a motor drive (chapter 1).
The measuring element in the feedback path that converts the output into a comparable signal (chapter 1).
e(t) = r(t) − b(t), the reference r(t) minus the feedback signal b(t) (chapter 1).
A system whose input is set without measuring the output; no feedback path exists (chapter 1).
Single-input single-output, and multi-input multi-output systems with several references and several outputs (chapter 1).
For negative feedback, T = G/(1 + GH), where G is the forward-path transfer function and H the feedback-path transfer function (chapter 2).
S = (∂T/T)/(∂G/G); with negative feedback it becomes 1/(1 + GH), smaller than 1 (chapter 2).
The frequency range over which the closed-loop gain stays near its low-frequency value; negative feedback widens it by (1 + GH) (chapter 2).
Feedback added with the same sign as the reference; loop gain 1 − GH, which reduces gain and pushes the system toward instability (chapter 2).
G(s) = Y(s)/R(s) for a linear time-invariant system with all initial conditions zero (chapter 3).
A transfer function whose numerator degree is less than its denominator degree (chapter 3).
m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = f(t), with m in kg, c in N·s/m, k in N/m and f in N (chapter 4).
Force ↔ voltage, velocity ↔ current, mass ↔ inductance, damper ↔ resistance, spring ↔ 1/capacitance (chapter 5).
e_b(t) = K_b ω(t); the voltage generated in the armature of a rotating machine, opposing the applied voltage (chapter 6).
R_th = ΔT/q, temperature difference in K divided by heat flow in W (chapter 7).
Replacing series, parallel and feedback blocks by single equivalent blocks to obtain one overall transfer function (chapter 8).
A path from the source node to the sink node that does not repeat any node (chapter 9).
Two loops that share no node; their gain product appears with a plus sign in the Mason formula (chapter 9).

takeaways: Open-loop control sets the input blindly; closed-loop control measures the output and acts on the error, so it can correct what it did not predict.
Negative feedback trades forward gain for wider bandwidth, smaller sensitivity to parameter drift and weaker disturbance and noise effects.
A transfer function exists only for linear time-invariant systems with zero initial conditions; it is the Laplace ratio of output to input.
Translational and rotational mechanical systems both follow the same form: inertia times acceleration plus damping plus stiffness equals the applied force or torque.
Force-voltage and force-current analogies let a mechanical model be solved with ordinary circuit analysis, giving the same transfer function.
In a DC servomotor the coupling is through the torque constant K_t and the back-emf constant K_b, which are numerically equal in SI units.
Thermal, liquid-level and pneumatic systems reduce to resistance-capacitance networks, often first order.
Block diagram reduction and Mason's gain formula are two routes to the same overall transfer function; the signal flow graph is usually faster for heavily interconnected systems.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to draw the block diagram or signal flow graph, then derive and reduce it to a single transfer function, so keep every step of the algebra visible.

bank.q: Draw the block diagrams of open-loop and closed-loop control systems. Explain each block, and give one Indian everyday example of each.
outline: Open-loop: reference → controller → actuator → plant → output; no sensor, no comparison.
Closed-loop: summing point forms e = r − b, controller acts on e, sensor in feedback path closes the loop.
Example open-loop: time-based traffic signal switching; example closed-loop: room air conditioner with a thermostat.
State advantages and disadvantages of each: simplicity and cost versus accuracy and disturbance rejection.

bank.q: Explain the effects of negative feedback on overall gain, bandwidth, disturbance, noise and stability of a control system.
outline: Overall gain falls from G to G/(1 + GH).
Bandwidth rises by the factor (1 + GH); the gain-bandwidth product stays roughly constant.
Disturbance and noise entering inside the loop are attenuated by 1/(1 + GH); noise in the feedback path is not.
Sensitivity to forward-path parameter changes falls to 1/(1 + GH).
Stability margin generally improves, but too much loop gain or added phase shift can cause instability.

bank.q: Define the transfer function of a linear time-invariant system. State its assumptions and classify transfer functions as proper, strictly proper and improper with one example each.
outline: Definition: ratio of Laplace transform of output to Laplace transform of input, all initial conditions zero.
Assumptions: linear, time-invariant, lumped parameters, zero initial conditions.
Proper: numerator degree equals denominator degree, for example (s+2)/(s+5).
Strictly proper: numerator degree less than denominator degree, for example 1/(s²+3s+2).
Improper: numerator degree greater than denominator degree, for example s²/(s+1); not realisable with pure differentiators alone.

bank.q: State the force-voltage and force-current analogies for a mechanical translational system, and tabulate the analogous electrical quantities.
outline: Write m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = f and compare with the mesh equation L q̈ + R q̇ + (1/C) q = v.
Force-voltage: force ↔ voltage, velocity ↔ current, mass ↔ inductance, damper ↔ resistance, spring ↔ 1/capacitance.
Force-current: force ↔ current, velocity ↔ voltage, mass ↔ capacitance, damper ↔ 1/resistance, spring ↔ 1/inductance.
Note that the two analogies are duals; either gives the same characteristic equation.

bank.q: A mass m is connected to a fixed wall through a spring k and a viscous damper c in parallel. A force f(t) is applied to the mass. Derive the transfer function X(s)/F(s).
outline: Free-body diagram: spring force k x and damper force c ẋ oppose the applied force.
Newton's second law: m ẍ = f − c ẋ − k x.
Take Laplace with zero initial conditions: (m s² + c s + k) X(s) = F(s).
Result X(s)/F(s) = 1/(m s² + c s + k); state natural frequency ω_n = √(k/m) and damping ratio ζ = c/(2√(km)).

bank.q: A rotational system has a moment of inertia J on a shaft with torsional stiffness K and viscous friction coefficient D, driven by a torque T(t). Derive the transfer function θ(s)/T(s).
outline: Rotational Newton's law: J θ̈ = T − D θ̇ − K θ.
Laplace with zero initial conditions: (J s² + D s + K) θ(s) = T(s).
Result θ(s)/T(s) = 1/(J s² + D s + K); units J in kg·m², D in N·m·s/rad, K in N·m/rad.

bank.q: For a separately excited DC servomotor, derive the transfer function θ(s)/V_a(s) with the load inertia and viscous friction included.
outline: Armature circuit: V_a = R_a i_a + L_a di_a/dt + e_b, with e_b = K_b ω.
Torque: T = K_t i_a, mechanical equation J ω̇ + D ω = T.
Eliminate i_a and use ω = dθ/dt.
Result θ(s)/V_a(s) = K_t / [s(L_a s + R_a)(J s + D) + K_t K_b s].
Note K_t = K_b in SI units; state the motor time constant and the mechanical time constant.

bank.q: Reduce a given block diagram containing a take-off point and a summing point (a standard three-loop configuration) to a single transfer function using block diagram reduction rules.
outline: Identify series blocks and multiply their transfer functions.
Identify parallel blocks and add or subtract them.
Move a take-off point ahead of or behind a block by multiplying or dividing by that block transfer function.
Combine the innermost feedback loop using G/(1 + GH).
Repeat outward and present the final single block.

bank.q: Draw the signal flow graph of a given block diagram and find the overall transfer function using Mason's gain formula.
outline: Convert every summing point and take-off point into a node; blocks become branches with gain.
List all forward paths and their path gains P₁, P₂, ...
List all individual loops and loop gains L₁, L₂, ... and identify non-touching pairs.
Compute Δ = 1 − ΣLᵢ + ΣLᵢLⱼ − ... and Δₖ for each forward path.
Apply T = (1/Δ) Σ Pₖ Δₖ and check against block reduction.

bank.q: Derive the transfer function H(s)/Q_in(s) of a single tank of cross-section A with a linear outlet resistance R, and find its time constant.
outline: Mass balance: A dh/dt = q_in − q_out.
Linear outlet: q_out = h/R.
Hence A dh/dt + h/R = q_in, giving (A R s + 1) H(s) = R Q_in(s).
Transfer function R/(AR s + 1), first order, time constant τ = AR in seconds.

bank.q: Show that negative feedback reduces the sensitivity of the overall gain to changes in the forward-path gain, and evaluate the price paid for this reduction.
outline: Start from T = G/(1 + GH); differentiate with respect to G.
Obtain S = 1/(1 + GH), so the fractional change in T is 1/(1 + GH) times that in G.
Example: with GH = 99, a 10 % rise in G gives about 0.1 % rise in T.
Price: forward gain drops by the same factor and the system needs a larger amplifier, more hardware and a wider bandwidth, which admits more high-frequency noise.

bank.q: A disturbance d(t) enters at the plant input and separately at the plant output. Analyse its effect on the output for open-loop and closed-loop operation and compare.
outline: Plant input disturbance: output due to d is G_d/(1 + GH), attenuated by the loop.
Output-side disturbance: output due to d is 1/(1 + GH) only if the sensor sees it; otherwise it is not corrected.
Open-loop case: the output is G_d d with no attenuation.
Conclusion: feedback suppresses disturbances inside the loop and leaves those in the feedback path unchanged.

bank.q: For a given mechanical translational system, draw the force-voltage analogous circuit, find the transfer function by circuit analysis, and judge whether the analogy or a direct mechanical solution is the better exam route.
outline: Write the mechanical equations of motion for each mass.
Map each mass to an inductance, damper to resistance and spring to inverse capacitance.
Write mesh equations of the analogous circuit and solve for the wanted variable.
Show the two transfer functions are identical.
Judge: the analogy is safer for coupled multi-mass problems; the direct route is faster for a single mass.

bank.q: Compare block diagram reduction and Mason's gain formula for finding the transfer function of a multi-loop system, and state when each method is preferable.
outline: Block reduction: graphical, rule based, error prone when take-off points must be shifted across summing points.
Mason: one formula T = (1/Δ)ΣPₖΔₖ, no redrawing, but loop identification must be exhaustive.
Mason's gain formula wins for many loops and non-touching loops; block reduction is clearer for a simple series-feedback chain.
Both must give the same characteristic polynomial, which is the check on the answer.

glossary.def: The component that turns a control signal into the physical effort applied to the plant, such as a motor or a valve.
The voltage induced in a rotating armature, proportional to speed, which opposes the applied armature voltage.
A drawing in which each system element is a block with its transfer function and arrows show the direction of signals.
A single directed line in a signal flow graph with a stated gain.
The denominator of the closed-loop transfer function set to zero; its roots decide the system's natural response and stability.
A system that measures its own output and uses the difference from the reference to drive the plant.
A viscous element producing a force or torque proportional to velocity, with coefficient c or D.
An unwanted input that enters the system and pushes the output away from the reference.
The blocks and sensor that carry the measured output back to the summing point.
The blocks from the summing point through the controller, actuator and plant to the output; also a node-free path from source to sink in a signal flow graph.
The integral transform F(s) = ∫₀^∞ f(t) e^(−st) dt that turns differential equations into algebraic equations in s.
The product of branch gains around a closed loop in a signal flow graph.
T = (1/Δ) Σ Pₖ Δₖ, where Pₖ is a forward-path gain and Δ the graph determinant.
A point in a signal flow graph representing a variable; the source node has only outgoing branches and the sink node only incoming ones.
Loops that share no node, so their gains multiply and appear with alternating sign in the graph determinant.
A system whose input is fixed without any measurement of the output.
The physical process whose output is to be controlled.
A small motor used as an actuator in control loops, modelled with armature resistance, inductance, torque constant and back-emf constant.
A directed graph whose nodes are system variables and whose branches carry transfer-function gains.
The fractional change in the overall transfer function divided by the fractional change in a parameter.
The measuring device in the feedback path, for example a tachometer or a thermocouple.
A junction where two or more signals are added or subtracted, marked with a cross and signs.
A point on a signal line from which the same signal is tapped and sent elsewhere.
The Laplace ratio of output to input of a linear time-invariant system with zero initial conditions.
